title: Student spending at Hartwell University
prompt: The chart below shows the average monthly spending of first-year and final-year students at Hartwell University on five items. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Average monthly spending by students, Hartwell University

sentences.text: The bar chart compares how much first-year and final-year students at Hartwell University spend each month on five types of expenditure.
sentences.why: Paraphrases the prompt without copying: "compares" replaces "shows", "spend each month" replaces "average monthly spending" and "types of expenditure" replaces "items". It gives no data and no opinion.

sentences.text: Overall, rent was the biggest expense for both groups of students, while books accounted for the smallest amount.
sentences.why: Gives the clearest feature of the chart with a stable top and bottom item. "While" contrasts the two ends of the ranking, and the lack of figures meets the Task Achievement requirement for an overview.

sentences.text: Final-year students spent more on rent and transport but less on the other three items.
sentences.why: The second overview point summarises the difference between the two groups. Grouping five categories into two patterns shows selection and comparison without using any numbers.

sentences.text: Rent and transport were the only two items on which final-year students spent more.
sentences.why: Topic sentence that groups the categories by direction of difference. It frames the paragraph with a clear selection and supports Coherence and Cohesion before any figures appear.

sentences.text: Rent rose from $420 for first-years to $480 for final-years, while transport spending increased from $90 to $130.
sentences.why: Reports both increases in one sentence with correct units. "Rose from ... to" and "increased from ... to" vary the verbs, and "while" links the two categories, supporting Lexical Resource and accuracy.

sentences.text: However, rent cost more than three times as much as transport for both groups.
sentences.why: Adds a comparison between categories rather than between groups. "More than three times as much as" is an accurate approximation (the ratios are about 4.7 and 3.7), showing grammatical range.

sentences.text: The rise in transport, at $40, was smaller in dollar terms than the $60 increase in rent, but proportionally larger.
sentences.why: Interprets the data with a concession structure. Comparing absolute and relative change shows analysis beyond description, and all the figures match the chart.

sentences.text: In contrast, final-year students spent less on food, books and entertainment.
sentences.why: Opens the second group with "in contrast" to signal the opposite pattern. Naming all three categories in the topic sentence gives a clear paragraph focus and supports Coherence.

sentences.text: Food spending dropped from $210 to $180, whereas books fell from $85 to just $40.
sentences.why: Contrasts a small fall with a large one using "whereas". "Dropped" and "fell" avoid repeating a verb, and "just" signals the low final figure, giving accurate, varied trend language.

sentences.text: Entertainment showed the largest decline in dollar terms, falling from $150 to $95.
sentences.why: Selects the biggest dollar change among the three and ranks it with a superlative. The participle "falling from ... to" adds the figures without a new sentence, earning grammatical range.

sentences.text: Books, the smallest item for both groups, fell to less than half of the first-year figure.
sentences.why: Closes by linking back to the overview point about books. The apposition adds the ranking, and "less than half" is a precise approximation because $40 is under half of $85.

analysis: The instruction is "Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant". Selecting means you must leave some data out; reporting all ten bars is a Task Achievement weakness.
What must be covered: the pattern for the two groups across five categories, the largest and smallest items, and which items rose and which fell between first-year and final-year students.

Paraphrase: "bar chart shows" becomes compares or illustrates; "average monthly spending" becomes how much students spend each month; "items" becomes categories or types of expenditure; "first-year and final-year" can stay as group names.
Key features: rent is highest for both (420 and 480); books are lowest (85 and 40); rent and transport are higher for final-years; food, books and entertainment are lower.
Group by direction of difference, not by the order of the axis: Body 1 for rent and transport (higher), Body 2 for food, books and entertainment (lower).
The chart does not say why spending differs. Do not mention income, loans or the length of the course; only report what the data show.

plan.idea: Paraphrase only: compares monthly spending by first-year and final-year students at Hartwell University on five types of expenditure. No data.
Rent is the biggest expense for both groups and books the smallest. Final-years spend more on rent and transport but less on the other three. No figures.
Rent $420 to $480 and transport $90 to $130. Rent over three times transport in both groups. Transport rise smaller in dollars, larger proportionally.
Food $210 to $180, books $85 to $40, entertainment $150 to $95 (largest fall). Books less than half the first-year figure.
